title: Writing code once for many types
objectives: Read a template error and predict which instantiations the compiler writes.

screens.title: The same function twice
screens.prose: You need the largest value of a vector of `int` volumes and of a vector of `double` prices. C++ checks types, so you write two functions.

lines: for (int x : xs) if (best < x) best = x;
for (double x : xs) if (best < x) best = x;
params.title: main.cpp

screens.question: Select all that apply: tap every line of the `double` version that differs from the `int` version.

hints.text: Compare line 6 with line 1, line 7 with line 2, and so on.
These two lines are the same in both.
Every line that names the element type differs: the signature, `best` and the loop variable.

feedback.correct: Only the type changes: lines 6, 7 and 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each line of the second function with the matching line of the first.

byKey.l9: `return best;` is the same in both versions.
byKey.l10: The closing brace is the same in both versions.
byKey.l1: That is in the `int` version. Compare the second function with the first.
byKey.l2: That is in the `int` version. Compare the second function with the first.
byKey.l3: That is in the `int` version. Compare the second function with the first.
byKey.l4: That is in the `int` version. Compare the second function with the first.
byKey.l5: That is in the `int` version. Compare the second function with the first.
byKey.l8: Line 8 declares `double x` in the loop, so the type appears there too.
byKey.l7: Line 7 declares `double best`, so it differs from line 2.

explain.text: The two bodies are the same idea with a different type in three places. A string version would repeat them again. C++ lets you write the type as a parameter instead.

screens.title: One template, many functions
screens.question: Select all that apply: tap every function the compiler writes for this program.

hints.text: Which types appear inside `std::vector<...>` in the calls?
Two calls use `std::vector<int>`.
Three types are used: `int`, `double` and `std::string`. One function is written for each.

feedback.correct: Three types used, three functions written.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write one function per type the calls use.

byKey.c: No call uses `std::vector<char>`, so no `char` version is written.
byKey.l: No call uses `std::vector<long>`, so no `long` version is written.
byKey.i: `max_of<int>` is used, twice. It is written once and called twice.
byKey.s: The last call uses `std::vector<std::string>`, so a string version is written.
byKey.d: The second call uses `std::vector<double>`, so a `double` version is written.

explain.text: At compile time the compiler writes one real function per type used: an **instantiation**. Two `int` calls share one function. Types never used cost nothing.

canvas.caption: Written at compile time: one function per type used

screens.title: Your first template
screens.prose: Now write one. Start the total at `T{}`, the type's empty value: 0 for numbers, `""` for a string. Then `+=` each element. The same source will add volumes, prices and even join tickers.
screens.question: Write `template <typename T> T sum_of(const std::vector<T>& xs)`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 7 hidden tests calling `sum_of` with vectors of `int`, `double`, `long long` and `std::string`.

hints.text: Write `template <typename T>` on the line before the function.
An empty vector must give the type's empty value.
`T total{}; for (const T& x : xs) total += x; return total;`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.compile: The compiler stopped. Check that `template <typename T>` comes right before the function, and that it returns `T`.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 adds doubles and expects 0.75. If you got 0, the total was an `int`: declare it as `T`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 joins strings. Start from `T{}`, not `0`: a `std::string` cannot start from a number.

explain.text: `T{}` is 0 for numbers and an empty string for `std::string`, so one start value works for every type. `+=` means addition for numbers and joining for strings. Each test's type got its own instantiation.

screens.title: One T per call
screens.prose: Here `T` is **deduced** from both arguments, and each argument has to agree.

params.title: Terminal
lines: main.cpp:7:16: error: no matching function for call to 'bigger'
main.cpp:2:3: note: candidate template ignored: deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' vs. 'double')

screens.question: Which call compiles and compares 3 with 2.5 without losing the half?

options.why: That is the failing call: from 3, `T` is `int`, and from 2.5 it is `double`. One `T` cannot be both.
That compiles, but `T` is `int`, so 2.5 becomes 2 before the comparison.
`bigger` has one type parameter, so it takes one type in the angle brackets.

hints.text: What type does `3` give `T`? What type does `2.5` give?
The note says the two deductions conflict.
Name `T` yourself in angle brackets; then both arguments convert to it.

feedback.correct: Naming `T` stops the deduction, and 3 converts to 3.0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the call where `T` is fixed and is a type that keeps the .5.

byKey.same: That is the failing call: from 3, `T` is `int`, and from 2.5 it is `double`. One `T` cannot be both.

explain.text: Each argument proposes a `T`, and they must agree. Writing `bigger<double>` fixes `T`, so the `int` 3 converts to 3.0. `bigger(3.0, 2.5)` works too.

screens.title: Reading a template error
screens.prose:
`std::sort` is a template, compiled again for every type you sort. Sorting `Quote`s, which have no `<`, fails deep inside the library. The real message runs to 359 lines; here are the first lines.

```cpp
std::vector<Quote> qs{{100.2, 100.4}, {99.9, 100.1}};
std::sort(qs.begin(), qs.end());   // line 11
```

lines: /usr/include/c++/v1/__algorithm/comp.h:41:18: error: invalid operands to binary expression ('const Quote' and 'const Quote')
/usr/include/c++/v1/__debug_utils/strict_weak_ordering_check.h:43:31: note: in instantiation of function template specialization 'std::__less<>::operator()<Quote, Quote>' requested here
/usr/include/c++/v1/__algorithm/sort.h:939:8: note: in instantiation of function template specialization 'std::__check_strict_weak_ordering_sorted<Quote *, std::__less<void, void>>' requested here

/usr/include/c++/v1/__algorithm/sort.h:945:8: note: in instantiation of function template specialization 'std::__sort_impl<std::_ClassicAlgPolicy, std::__wrap_iter<Quote *>, std::__less<void, void>>' requested here
/usr/include/c++/v1/__algorithm/sort.h:951:8: note: in instantiation of function template specialization 'std::sort<std::__wrap_iter<Quote *>, std::__less<void, void>>' requested here
main.cpp:11:10: note: in instantiation of function template specialization 'std::sort<std::__wrap_iter<Quote *>>' requested here
fatal error: too many errors emitted, stopping now [-ferror-limit=]
params.title: Terminal

screens.question: Tap the two lines that matter: what is missing, and which line of your code asked for it.

hints.text: Look for the first `error:` and for the first line that names `main.cpp`.
This is the first error.
Line 5 says `<` has no meaning for two `Quote`s. Line 20 points at `main.cpp:11`, your call to `std::sort`.

feedback.correct: The first error says what is missing; the `main.cpp` note says where you asked.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Skip the library paths and look for `error:` and `main.cpp`.

byKey.l7: That is a library file's path, an `instantiation` note. The cause is in the first `error:` line.
byKey.l11: That is a library file's path, an `instantiation` note. Find the line that names `main.cpp`.
byKey.l14: That is a library file's path, an `instantiation` note. Find the line that names `main.cpp`.
byKey.l2: That line only says which header the error is in. Find the first `error:`.
byKey.l23: Later errors repeat the same cause. Read the first one.

explain.text: Line 5: `<` is missing for `Quote`. Line 20: your line 11 asked for it. Everything between is the chain of templates from your call down to the comparison: give `Quote` an `operator<`, or pass `std::sort` a comparison.

screens.title: A class template
screens.prose: A class can be a template too: `Series<T>` holds a vector of `T`. Here it holds tickers, where a mean makes no sense.

lines: for (const T& x : xs_) total += x;
params.title: main.cpp

screens.question: Does this program build?

options.text: Yes: nothing calls `mean`, so it is never compiled for `std::string`

options.why: You expected every member to be checked for `std::string`. A class template's member function is compiled only when called, and nothing calls `names.mean()`.
Nothing in the template says so. `T` can be any type until a member uses it in a way the type cannot do.

hints.text: Which member functions does `main` call?
`mean` is defined here but never called.
Only `push` is called, and pushing a string is fine.

feedback.correct: It builds: `mean` is never instantiated for `std::string`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which members `main` actually calls.

byKey.no: You expected every member to be checked for `std::string`. A class template's member function is compiled only when called, and nothing calls `names.mean()`.

explain.text: A template's body is checked for a type only when that code is used. Add `names.mean();` and clang reports `invalid operands ... ('std::string' and 'size_type')` at line 8. So a template is only proven for the types you have actually compiled it with.

screens.title: The mean of whole numbers

lines: for (const T& x : xs_) total += x;
params.title: main.cpp

screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected a fractional mean. With `T = int` the total is an `int`, `mean` returns an `int`, and the division drops the half, as in level 1.
Integer division does not round: 4001 / 2 is 2000, the fraction thrown away.

options.text: A compile error: `int` cannot be divided by a size
options.why: `int` divides by an unsigned size and compiles. The problem is the type of the answer.

hints.text: What is `T` here, and what does `mean` return?
This line divides a total of type `T`.
4001 / 2 in whole numbers is 2000.

feedback.correct: `T mean()` with `T = int` is an integer division.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the type of `total / xs_.size()`.

byKey.exact: You expected a fractional mean. With `T = int` the total is an `int`, `mean` returns an `int`, and the division drops the half, as in level 1.

screens.title: A number as a parameter
screens.question: How many units does `FixedPoint<4>` store for the rate 1.2345?

hints.text: How many units of $10^{-4}$ make 1.2345?
The first row multiplies 12.34 by $10^2$.
Multiply by $10^4 = 10000$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the value by $10^{\text{Places}}$.

byKey.two: You used two places, as for pence. `FixedPoint<4>` keeps four.
byKey.raw: That is the value itself. The class stores a whole number of $10^{-4}$ units.

explain.text: `Places` is fixed at compile time, so `FixedPoint<2>` and `FixedPoint<4>` are different types. Adding pence to an FX rate by mistake becomes a compile error. `std::array<double, 5>` uses a number parameter the same way.

screens.title: Templates in general
screens.question: What are `std::vector<double>` and `std::vector<int>`?

options.text: Two classes the compiler wrote from one template
One class that can hold any type, like a Python list
options.why: A Python list holds any object at run time. C++ writes separate code for each element type at compile time.

options.text: Two classes the library authors wrote by hand
options.why: The library ships one template; your program's uses decide which classes get written.

options.text: One class that checks the element type at run time
options.why: There is no run-time check: the element type is part of the class, fixed when it compiles.

hints.text: Recall the graph of `max_of<T>` and its instantiations.
`vector` is a class template, instantiated once per element type you use.

feedback.correct: The standard library is almost entirely templates.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of `max_of<T>` and the functions written from it.

explain.text: `std::vector`, `std::map`, `std::sort` and `std::unique_ptr` are all templates. That is how one library serves every type, with no run-time cost: each use is compiled for its exact type.

screens.title: A rolling window for prices and volumes
screens.prose: A signal uses the mean of the last $n$ prices, and a volume filter the mean of the last $n$ volumes. One class template serves both. Volumes are held as `double` here, so the mean keeps its fraction. An empty window has no mean.
screens.question: Write the constructor's check (`n` above 0), `push`, which keeps only the last `n` values, and `T mean() const`, which refuses an empty window.

examples.setup: Window<double> w(3); w.push(100.0); w.push(101.0); w.push(102.0); w.push(106.0);

tests.setup: Window<double> w(3); w.push(100.0); w.push(101.0); w.push(102.0); w.push(106.0);
Window<double> w(3); w.push(100.0); w.push(101.0); w.push(102.0); w.push(106.0);

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 9 hidden tests with `Window<double>`: prices, volumes, a window of 1, and two that pass only if the program stops.

hints.text: In `push`, add the value, then drop the oldest if there are more than `n_`.
After the fourth push, the 100 is gone.
`xs_.push_back(x); if (static_cast<int>(xs_.size()) > n_) xs_.erase(xs_.begin());` and in `mean`, refuse `xs_.empty()`, then sum from `T{}`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 pushes 4 values into a window of 3 and expects 103. Drop the oldest value.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 asks for the mean of an empty window. Refuse it before dividing by zero.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 builds a window of size 0. Refuse it in the constructor.

explain.text: `Window<double>` serves prices and volumes alike, and `Window<FixedPoint<2>>` would work once it has `+=` and `/`. Erasing the front costs a shift of $n$ values, fine for small windows; level 4's containers do it in constant time.

ideas: A template takes a type (or a number) as a parameter. The compiler writes one instantiation per set of parameters you use, at compile time.
`T` is deduced from the arguments, and every argument must agree; name it yourself (`bigger<double>`) when they do not. A template's body is checked only when it is used.
In a template error, read the first `error:` line and the line that names your own file; the rest is the path between them.

formula.name: Instantiation
formula.note: One function per type used; none for types never used.

summary.trap: Returning `T` from a mean makes `Series<int>` divide in whole numbers: 4001 / 2 gives 2000. Return `double`.

quiz.prose:
With the `max_of` template from this lesson:

```cpp
max_of(std::vector<std::string>{"BARC", "AZN", "VOD", "LLOY"})
```
quiz.question: What does it return?

options.why: `<` on strings compares letter by letter, not by length. V comes after L.
That is only the starting `best`. Any later string that compares greater replaces it.

options.text: A compile error: strings have no maximum
options.why: `std::string` has `<`, alphabetical order, so the template compiles for it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. `<` on strings is alphabetical order.

explain.text: For `std::string`, `best < x` compares alphabetically, so the maximum is the last ticker in the alphabet: VOD.

quiz.question: How many functions does the compiler write from `sum_of`?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the different element types, not the calls.

byKey.calls: You counted calls. The two `int` calls share one instantiation.
byKey.one: A template is not one function: each type used gets its own.

explain.text: The two `int` calls share `sum_of<int>`. With `double` and `long long`, that makes three instantiations.

quiz.prose: You declare `template <typename T> T sum_of(const std::vector<T>&);` in `stats.h` and define it in `stats.cpp`. `main.cpp` includes `stats.h` and calls `sum_of` with a `std::vector<double>`. Both files compile.
quiz.question: What happens at the link step?

options.text: An undefined reference to `sum_of<double>`: no file ever wrote it

options.why: `stats.cpp` never sees a `double` call, so it writes no `sum_of<double>`. `main.cpp` sees the call but not the body.
The declaration is enough to compile the call. The missing function shows up only when linking.

feedback.correct: A template's body must be visible where it is used, so it goes in the header.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which file could write `sum_of<double>`?

explain.text: An instantiation is written where the body and the type meet. Here they never meet, so the linker finds no `sum_of<double>`. Put template definitions in the header.

quiz.question: What are `a` and `b`?

options.text: Both calls stop: the vectors are empty
options.why: The loop runs zero times and the function returns its start value, `T{}`.
`T{}` for a string is the empty string, not the text 0.

feedback.correct: An empty sum is the type's empty value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `T{}` give for each type?

explain.text: With no elements the loop never runs, so the result is `T{}`: 0.0 for `double` and `""` for `std::string`. `auto` takes each type from the call.
